Kubernetes · apps/v1 · Deployment · Argo Rollouts · Istio

Deployment strategies, from Recreate to Shadow traffic

How Kubernetes replaces one version of a workload with the next: the native Recreate and RollingUpdate strategies, and the Blue/Green, Canary, A/B and Shadow patterns built from Services, ingress-nginx, Istio, Argo Rollouts and Flagger. Every manifest is apply-ready and traced on the three-zone Jahez cluster.

apps/v1networking.istio.io/v1argoproj.io/v1alpha1jahez-prodme-central-1a/b/cghcr.io/jahez
I
Part I · High Level
Definitions, the problems, the solution, comparisons, architecture and the rollout loop.
1.1 · 1. Foundations

Introduction

In one sentence

A deployment strategy is the plan for replacing the running version of a workload with a new one, without losing requests and with a way back.

A deployment strategy decides how many new Pods start, how many old Pods stop and in which order, who receives traffic during the change, what has to be true before the change continues, and how you return to the old version. Kubernetes ships two strategies inside the Deployment controller (part of kube-controller-manager): Recreate and RollingUpdate. Everything else — Blue/Green, Canary, A/B and Shadow — is a pattern you build from Services, Ingress controllers such as ingress-nginx, a service mesh such as Istio, and progressive-delivery controllers such as Argo Rollouts and Flagger.

✓ It is

  • The spec.strategy of a Deployment (native), or a set of objects plus a routing rule (composed)
  • A decision about capacity, risk and rollback time
  • Gated by readiness and, optionally, by metric analysis
  • Recorded as revisions you can undo

✕ It is not

  • A CI pipeline: CI builds ghcr.io/jahez/menu-service:v2.4.0; the strategy decides how it replaces v1.9.3
  • A database migration tool: schema changes need their own expand/contract plan
  • A feature flag: it routes whole versions, not code paths inside one binary
  • Autoscaling: HPA changes replicas and never creates a revision

Definitions

Deployment

A Deployment is the object that says "keep N copies of this Pod template running, and when I change the template, replace the old copies the way strategy says".

🎯 Why it exists

Pods are mortal and have no upgrade logic. Something must own them, keep the count right and swap versions safely. That is the Deployment controller inside kube-controller-manager.

📄 What it looks like
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: menu-service-deployment
spec:
  replicas: 4
  strategy:
    type: RollingUpdate
⚙ What Kubernetes does with it

It never touches Pods directly. It creates a ReplicaSet per template version and scales those up and down.

Before
image: menu-service:v1.9.3
ReplicaSet …-7d9f8c6b5  4/4
→
After
image: menu-service:v2.4.0
ReplicaSet …-6b8f9d7c4  4/4
ReplicaSet …-7d9f8c6b5  0/0
📍 Where it lives

Namespace jahez-prod, stored in etcd; the file lives in deploy/02-rolling-update/.

⚠ Watch out

spec.selector is immutable. Changing labels later means deleting and recreating the Deployment, which is a Recreate in disguise.

ReplicaSet

A ReplicaSet keeps an exact number of Pods from one template version alive. Its name ends with the template hash.

🎯 Why it exists

Two versions need two counters. The Deployment moves replicas from the old ReplicaSet to the new one; that hand-off is the rollout.

📄 What it looks like
kind: ReplicaSet
metadata:
  name: menu-service-deployment-6b8f9d7c4
  labels:
    pod-template-hash: 6b8f9d7c4
⚙ What Kubernetes does with it

The ReplicaSet controller creates or deletes Pods until the count matches spec.replicas, in slow-start batches of 1, 2, 4, 8…

Before
replicas: 0  (new, just created)
→
After
replicas: 4  (4 Pods Running)
📍 Where it lives

Created and named by the Deployment controller. You never write one by hand.

⚠ Watch out

Editing a ReplicaSet directly is undone at once: the Deployment owns it and resets it.

Revision

A revision is one numbered version of the Pod template. Each kept ReplicaSet carries its number in deployment.kubernetes.io/revision.

🎯 Why it exists

It is what makes kubectl rollout undo possible: going back means "scale the ReplicaSet of revision 7 up again".

📄 What it looks like
metadata:
  annotations:
    deployment.kubernetes.io/revision: "8"
    kubernetes.io/change-cause: "v2.4.0 · new menu layout"
⚙ What Kubernetes does with it

A new template hash makes a new revision. Scaling or changing strategy does not.

Before
REVISION  CHANGE-CAUSE
7         v1.9.3
→
After
REVISION  CHANGE-CAUSE
7         v1.9.3
8         v2.4.0 · new menu layout
📍 Where it lives

On the ReplicaSets; listed by kubectl rollout history. Count capped by revisionHistoryLimit.

⚠ Watch out

kubectl scale and kubectl set resources on the same image behave differently: only template changes create revisions.

Rollout

A rollout is the act of moving from one revision to the next: Pods start, pass readiness, and old Pods stop, until the new ReplicaSet owns every replica.

🎯 Why it exists

You want one name for "the upgrade in progress" so you can watch it, pause it, resume it or undo it as a unit.

📄 What it looks like
status:
  conditions:
    - type: Progressing
      reason: NewReplicaSetAvailable
⚙ What Kubernetes does with it

The controller moves through windows bounded by maxSurge and maxUnavailable and records progress in status.conditions.

Before
updatedReplicas: 1
availableReplicas: 4
→
After
updatedReplicas: 4
availableReplicas: 4
📍 Where it lives

Triggered by any change under spec.template; watched with kubectl rollout status.

⚠ Watch out

A rollout that never becomes Available is not cancelled. It just sits there until progressDeadlineSeconds marks it failed.

maxSurge

maxSurge is how many Pods may run above replicas during a RollingUpdate. Count or percent (rounded up).

🎯 Why it exists

New Pods must start before old ones stop, or capacity dips. Surge pays for that overlap with extra resources.

📄 What it looks like
strategy:
  rollingUpdate:
    maxSurge: 1
⚙ What Kubernetes does with it

With 4 replicas and maxSurge: 1 the ceiling is 5 Pods: one new Pod at a time.

Before
Pods: 4 (v1)
→
After
Pods: 4 v1 + 1 v2 starting = 5
📍 Where it lives

Under spec.strategy.rollingUpdate; ignored by Recreate.

⚠ Watch out

Every surge Pod needs resources.requests free on a node. No room means a Pending Pod and a stuck rollout.

maxUnavailable

maxUnavailable is how many Pods may be missing below replicas during a RollingUpdate. Count or percent (rounded down).

🎯 Why it exists

Some services can lose a little capacity to finish faster; checkout cannot.

📄 What it looks like
strategy:
  rollingUpdate:
    maxUnavailable: 0
⚙ What Kubernetes does with it

With 4 replicas and maxUnavailable: 0 at least 4 Pods are always available.

Before
available: 4
→
After
available: never below 4
📍 Where it lives

Under spec.strategy.rollingUpdate.

⚠ Watch out

maxSurge: 0 together with maxUnavailable: 0 is rejected: the rollout could never move.

Ready vs Available

A Pod is Ready when its readinessProbe passes; it is Available when it has stayed Ready for minReadySeconds.

🎯 Why it exists

A Pod that is Ready for one second and then crashes should not let the rollout drain another old Pod.

📄 What it looks like
minReadySeconds: 10
readinessProbe:
  httpGet:
    path: /ready
    port: 8080
⚙ What Kubernetes does with it

Ready adds the Pod IP to the EndpointSlice (traffic flows). Available is what the rollout counts before it continues.

Before
Running, not Ready: no traffic
→
After
Ready 10s → Available: next window opens
📍 Where it lives

Ready: Pod status.conditions. Available: Deployment status.availableReplicas.

⚠ Watch out

No readinessProbe means Ready = "process started", so the rollout races ahead of a warming app.

Traffic split

A traffic split decides which share of requests reaches each version: by Pod count behind one Service, or by explicit weights in an Ingress or mesh.

🎯 Why it exists

Canary, A/B and shadow all need two versions live at once with control over who reaches which.

📄 What it looks like
route:
  - destination:
      host: menu-service
      subset: stable
    weight: 75
⚙ What Kubernetes does with it

A Service spreads evenly over Ready Pods (L4). ingress-nginx and Istio read headers, cookies and weights (L7).

Before
4 Pods v1 → 100% v1
→
After
3 v1 + 1 v2 → ≈25% v2 (ratio)
or weight 25 → exactly 25%
📍 Where it lives

Service selectors, Ingress annotations, Istio VirtualService.

⚠ Watch out

A ratio split cannot express 1% with 4 Pods. Exact small weights need L7 routing.

Stable and canary tracks

Two Deployments of the same app: stable (current) and canary (new), told apart by a track label.

🎯 Why it exists

Each track can be scaled, routed and rolled back on its own.

📄 What it looks like
labels:
  app: menu-service
  track: canary
⚙ What Kubernetes does with it

A shared Service selects only app, so it reaches both tracks; DestinationRule subsets select by track.

Before
stable 4 · canary 0
→
After
stable 3 · canary 1
📍 Where it lives

deploy/04-canary/.

⚠ Watch out

If both tracks share the same selector labels the two Deployments fight over the same Pods. Keep track in each selector.

Active and preview Services

In Blue/Green, the active Service sends users to one colour; the preview Service always points at the new colour for testing.

🎯 Why it exists

You want to test green with real cluster networking before any user reaches it.

📄 What it looks like
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: menu-active-service
spec:
  selector:
    version: blue
⚙ What Kubernetes does with it

Changing the active selector swaps the EndpointSlice in one write: the cutover.

Before
active → version: blue
→
After
active → version: green
📍 Where it lives

deploy/03-blue-green/, or managed by Argo Rollouts.

⚠ Watch out

Open connections to blue are not moved; they finish or break when blue is scaled down.

Analysis gate

An analysis gate is a metric check that must pass before a rollout continues, e.g. success rate ≥ 99% from Prometheus.

🎯 Why it exists

Readiness only says "the process is up". A version can be Ready and still return 500s.

📄 What it looks like
kind: AnalysisTemplate
spec:
  metrics:
    - name: success-rate
      successCondition: result[0] >= 0.99
⚙ What Kubernetes does with it

Argo Rollouts runs it as an AnalysisRun; Flagger runs it in its loop. Failure aborts and moves traffic back to stable.

Before
canary 25% · analysis Running
→
After
Successful → setWeight 50
Failed → abort, 0%
📍 Where it lives

deploy/argo-rollouts/analysis-templates.yaml.

⚠ Watch out

A query that returns no data is "inconclusive", not "pass". Test the query on today's traffic first.

Mirror (shadow)

A mirror sends a copy of each live request to the new version and throws its answer away.

🎯 Why it exists

You can watch v2 under the real Ramadan peak with zero user risk.

📄 What it looks like
mirror:
  host: menu-service
  subset: shadow
mirrorPercentage:
  value: 10.0
⚙ What Kubernetes does with it

The Istio sidecar duplicates the request asynchronously; the user only waits for v1.

Before
v1 gets 100%, v2 gets 0
→
After
v1 answers 100%
v2 receives a 10% copy
📍 Where it lives

deploy/06-shadow/.

⚠ Watch out

Copies run real code: writes, Mada charges and notifications happen twice unless the shadow is isolated (7.2).

1.2 · 1. Foundations

Problems or needs

In one sentence

Without strategies, shipping means delete-then-create: a gap, no memory of the old version, everyone exposed at once, no targeting and no safe load test.

Follow one Jahez release, menu-service v1.9.3 → v2.4.0, using only bare Pods and plain commands.

Life before deployment strategies5 steps
1

Ship v2 by deleting v1 first

  • The only tools are delete and create. Between them, zero Pods serve.
  • At lunch peak in Riyadh, a 60-second gap is thousands of failed menu loads.
by-hand.shmanual
kubectl -n jahez-prod delete pod -l app=menu-service        # 10:01 every Pod gone
kubectl -n jahez-prod apply -f menu-service-pod-v2.yaml      # 10:02 new Pods still pulling
kubectl -n jahez-prod get pods -w                            # wait and hope
‹ Back1 / 5
2

v2 is broken: how do we get back?

  • Nothing in the cluster remembers the previous template.
  • Going back is a second risky deploy, under pressure, with a second gap.
rollback-by-hand.shmanual
git log --oneline deploy/ | head                              # which commit was v1?
git show a1b2c3d:deploy/menu-service-pod.yaml > v1.yaml
kubectl -n jahez-prod delete pod -l app=menu-service
kubectl -n jahez-prod apply -f v1.yaml
2 / 5
3

A bad version reaches everyone at once

  • Readiness passing does not prove v2 is correct: it can be Ready and still return 500s.
  • You learn about the bug from the support queue, not from a small sample.
watch-and-pray.shmanual
kubectl -n jahez-prod apply -f menu-service-v2.yaml
kubectl -n jahez-prod logs -l app=menu-service -f | grep -c ' 500 '
3 / 5
4

Try a new menu layout only for beta users

  • A Service balances at L4 over every matching Pod: no headers, no cookies, no "same user, same version".
  • Product cannot measure basket size per variant because users flip between them.
mixed.shmanual
kubectl -n jahez-prod scale deploy/menu-v2 --replicas=1    # "about 20%", but random per request
curl -H 'x-jahez-beta: true' https://menu.jahez.sa/menu        # header ignored
4 / 5
5

Will v2 survive iftar peak?

  • Ramadan iftar traffic has request shapes and cache misses that staging never sees.
  • Without a way to copy live traffic, every performance regression is found by customers.
hope.shmanual
hey -z 5m -c 200 https://staging.menu.jahez.sa/menu   # not the real mix
kubectl -n jahez-prod apply -f menu-service-v2.yaml     # find out live

How each of these is solved → 1.3 Solution

5 / 5Done ✓
NeedWhy it hurts at Jahez
No downtime during a releaseMenu and checkout are on every order path
A fast, known way backA bad release at lunch peak must be undone in seconds
Limit who sees a new versionA bug should hit 1% of orders, not 100%
Send chosen users to a variantProduct tests layouts per city or per beta group
Test with real traffic, safelyIftar peaks cannot be reproduced in staging
1.3 · 1. Foundations

Solution

In one sentence

Kubernetes keeps every template version as a ReplicaSet and moves replicas between them behind a readiness gate; routing objects and analysis controllers then decide who sees which version and when to continue.

The solution in five steps

  1. Version the template. A Deployment turns every template change into a new ReplicaSet and a revision number. Going back = scaling an old ReplicaSet up again (fixes problem 2).
  2. Overlap, do not gap. RollingUpdate starts new Pods before stopping old ones, bounded by maxSurge / maxUnavailable (fixes problem 1).
  3. Gate on readiness. The rollout only continues when new Pods are Ready and Available for minReadySeconds.
  4. Split traffic on purpose. Two Deployments plus a Service selector, an ingress-nginx canary Ingress or an Istio VirtualService decide who reaches v2 (fixes problems 3 and 4).
  5. Gate on metrics or copies. Argo Rollouts and Flagger advance only when Prometheus says v2 is healthy; Istio mirroring copies live load to a shadow (fixes problems 3 and 5).

The real folder tree

menu-service/
└─ deploy/
   ├─ 01-recreate/        menu-migrator-deployment.yaml
   ├─ 02-rolling-update/  menu-service-deployment.yaml · rolling-profiles.yaml
   ├─ 03-blue-green/      menu-blue-green.yaml · cutover.sh · menu-blue-green-application.yaml
   ├─ 04-canary/          menu-canary.yaml · menu-canary-istio.yaml · *.sh
   ├─ 05-ab-testing/      menu-ab-deployments.yaml · ingress-nginx/ · istio/
   ├─ 06-shadow/          menu-shadow.yaml · menu-shadow-isolation.yaml
   ├─ argo-rollouts/      menu-rollout-blue-green.yaml · menu-rollout-canary.yaml · analysis-templates.yaml
   └─ flagger/            menu-canary-flagger.yaml

What one RollingUpdate apply does, in numbers

For menu-service-deployment with replicas: 4, maxSurge: 1, maxUnavailable: 0, minReadySeconds: 10 and a Pod that becomes Ready in ~8 s:

MeasureValueWhy
Pods ever running at once54 + maxSurge 1
Pods available, minimum44 − maxUnavailable 0
Windows4one new Pod per window
Time per window≈ 18–25 spull + 8 s ready + 10 s minReadySeconds + drain
Total rollout≈ 1.5 min4 windows; fails after 300 s with no progress
Revisions kept10revisionHistoryLimit

One tab per strategy

Solves "two versions must never overlap". Keeps the gap, so use it for workers and migrations only.

snippetdeploy/01-recreate
strategy:
  type: Recreate

Solves the gap and the missing way back (revisions + rollout undo).

snippetdeploy/02-rolling-update
strategy:
  type: RollingUpdate
  rollingUpdate:
    maxSurge: 1
    maxUnavailable: 0

Solves "instant cutover and instant way back" at the cost of 2× capacity.

snippetdeploy/03-blue-green
selector:
  app: menu-service
  version: green

Solves "a bad version reaches everyone": only a slice sees it until metrics clear it.

snippetdeploy/04-canary
steps:
  - setWeight: 25
  - pause:
      duration: 10m

Solves "send chosen users to a variant" with header, cookie, path or weight rules.

snippetdeploy/05-ab-testing
match:
  - headers:
      x-jahez-beta:
        exact: "true"

Solves "test under real load safely": v2 sees production traffic, users never see v2.

snippetdeploy/06-shadow
mirror:
  host: menu-service
  subset: shadow

Problem (1.2)Solved byHow
① Delete-then-create gapRollingUpdate · Blue/GreenNew Pods are Ready before old ones stop

③ Bad version reaches everyoneCanary + analysisOnly a slice sees v2 until success ≥ 99%

1.4 · 1. Foundations

Comparisons

In one sentence

Pick by three questions: can two versions overlap, how much spare capacity do you have, and do you need to choose who sees v2?

Every strategy compared

StrategyNative?DowntimePeak reserved (4 × 1 GiB)RollbackTraffic controlNeeds
Recreateyesyes · gap4 GiB → 0 → 4 GiBanother Recreate (another gap)all or nothingDeployment
RollingUpdateyesno5 GiB (surge 1) · 8 GiB (fast)rollout undo (re-rolls)none, emergentDeployment
Blue/Greennono8 GiB for the whole overlapinstant flipall at once2 Deployments + Service
Canarynono4–6 GiB (ratio) · 8 GiB (additive)scale canary 0 / weight 0% by ratio or weight2 Deployments + Service or mesh
A/Bnono6 GiB plateau for daysremove the ruleheader · cookie · path · weightingress-nginx or Istio
Shadownono8 GiB while mirroringn/a: users never saw v2copy, answer discardedIstio

Recreate vs Blue/Green — same shape, minus the gap

DimensionRecreateBlue/Green
Switch styleAll at onceAll at once same
Users see one version at a timeYesYes same
Downtime0 Pods during the gapnone · instant flip
New version comes upOnly after old is destroyedFully, beside the old, before the flip
Versions running at onceneverboth, during the overlap
Extra capacitynone (drops to 0)2× during overlap
Verify before trafficNoYes · preview Service
RollbackAnother RecreateFlip selector back
Best forIncompatible schema, singletonsZero-downtime cutover with instant rollback
Serving
v1 (blue) serving
Downtime
Flip
✕ Not a free swap

People pick Recreate because two versions must never run together: an incompatible schema, an exclusive lock, a singleton. Blue/Green runs both during the overlap, so it breaks that guarantee.

Canary vs RollingUpdate — the control plane, not the Pod math

DimensionRollingUpdateCanary
Advance decided byReadiness probe: "is the process up?"Observed behaviour: error rate, p99, checkout success
Who drives itDeployment controller, automaticYou, Argo Rollouts or Flagger, gated
Dwell / bakeNonePauses at each weight
Topology1 Deployment, 2 ReplicaSets2 Deployments or a Rollout
Traffic controlEmergent from Pod ratioExplicit % / header with a mesh
Bad version reachesEveryone, if it is ReadyOnly the canary slice
RollbackRe-roll in reverseWeight to 0 / scale canary to 0
Footprint+maxSurgeRatio: flat · additive: up to 2×
◆ A spectrum

kubectl rollout pause after the first window turns a RollingUpdate into a manual canary. What makes it a canary is gating on observation.

When to choose what

▲ Quick rule

Stateless service, normal release → RollingUpdate. Instant cutover and rollback, 2× affordable → Blue/Green. Expose a small % first → Canary. Test a product idea on a segment → A/B. Real load, zero user risk → Shadow. Incompatible schema or singleton → Recreate behind a maintenance window.

2.1 · 2. Architecture and workflows

Architecture

In one sentence

A rollout is a relay: CI pushes an image, the API server stores the change, controllers create ReplicaSets and Pods, kubelets start them, and Services, ingress-nginx or Istio decide who reaches them.

PartWhereWhat it does in a rolloutUsed by
API server + etcdcontrol planeValidates the change, bumps metadata.generation, stores revisions and statusall
Deployment controllerkube-controller-managerHashes the template, creates the new ReplicaSet, moves replicas window by windowRecreate, RollingUpdate, all Deployments
ReplicaSet controllerkube-controller-managerCreates and deletes Pods in slow-start batchesall
Schedulercontrol planePlaces surge Pods on a node with free requests, honours zone spreadall
kubeleteach nodePulls ghcr.io/jahez/…, starts containers, runs probes, sends SIGTERMall
EndpointSlice controllerkube-controller-managerAdds Ready Pod IPs, removes terminating onesall routing
Servicekube-proxy on nodesL4 spread over selected Ready PodsRollingUpdate, Blue/Green, ratio canary
ingress-nginxedge PodsL7 canary Ingress: header, cookie, weightA/B, edge canary
Istio sidecarsevery meshed PodExact weights, matches and mirroringCanary, A/B, Shadow
Argo Rollouts / Flaggerown controller PodsRun steps, query Prometheus, promote or abortprogressive delivery
Prometheusmonitoring namespaceSupplies success rate and latency to gatesCanary, Blue/Green analysis

Which parts light up per strategy

2.2 · 2. Architecture and workflows

Repository layout

In one sentence

Every strategy lives in its own folder under deploy/; each folder is a complete alternative you apply on its own, never together.

① git repo · github.com/jahez/menu-service③ registry · ghcr.io/jahez④ cluster · jahez-prod
📁 menu-service/deploy/
📁 01-recreate/

Deployment · Servicedeploy/01-recreate/menu-migrator-deployment.yaml
In one sentence

A migration worker that must never run two versions at once.

menu-migrator-deployment.yamlkubectl apply -f
# Internal migration worker: one version at a time, a short gap is acceptable
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: menu-migrator-deployment
  namespace: jahez-prod
  labels:
    app: menu-migrator
    tier: backend
spec:
  # ① What to run?
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: menu-migrator
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: menu-migrator
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: migrator
          image: ghcr.io/jahez/menu-migrator:v2
          ports:
            - containerPort: 8080
          env:
            - name: DB_HOST
              value: "postgres-rw.jahez-prod.svc"
            - name: REGION
              value: "me-central-1"
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /healthz
              port: 8080
            initialDelaySeconds: 5
            periodSeconds: 5
  # ② How to replace the old Pods?
  strategy:
    type: Recreate                       # kill all, then create all; no rollingUpdate block
  # ④ What to keep for going back?
  revisionHistoryLimit: 5
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: menu-migrator-service
  namespace: jahez-prod
spec:
  selector:                              # version-agnostic: matches v1 and v2
    app: menu-migrator
  ports:
    - port: 80
      targetPort: 8080
What each block does
  • ① What to run? → replicas, selector, matchLabels, app, template, metadata
  • ② How to replace the old Pods? → strategy, type
  • ④ What to keep for going back? → revisionHistoryLimit, apiVersion, kind, metadata, name, namespace

Deployment · Servicedeploy/02-rolling-update/menu-service-deployment.yaml
In one sentence

menu-service with every rollout field set: the reference file of 3.0.

menu-service-deployment.yamlkubectl apply -f
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: menu-service-deployment
  namespace: jahez-prod
  labels:
    app: menu-service
  annotations:
    kubernetes.io/change-cause: "v2.4.0 · new menu layout"   # shown by rollout history
spec:
  # ① What to run?
  replicas: 4
  selector:                              # immutable after create
    matchLabels:
      app: menu-service
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: menu-service                # must match the selector
    spec:
      terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 30
      containers:
        - name: menu
          image: ghcr.io/jahez/menu-service:v2.4.0   # changing this starts a rollout
          ports:
            - containerPort: 8080
          resources:
            requests:
              cpu: "250m"
              memory: "1Gi"
            limits:
              cpu: "500m"
              memory: "3Gi"
          readinessProbe:                # the gate every rollout waits on
            httpGet:
              path: /ready
              port: 8080
            periodSeconds: 5
  # ② How to replace the old Pods?
  strategy:
    type: RollingUpdate
    # ③ How fast and how safe?
    rollingUpdate:
      maxSurge: 1# at most replicas + 1 = 5 Pods
      maxUnavailable: 0# never fewer than 4 available
  minReadySeconds: 10# Ready for 10s before it counts
  progressDeadlineSeconds: 300# no progress for 5 min = failed
  paused: false
  # ④ What to keep for going back?
  revisionHistoryLimit: 10# old ReplicaSets kept for rollout undo
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: menu-service
  namespace: jahez-prod
spec:
  # ① Which Pods get traffic?
  selector:
    app: menu-service                    # no version key: spans old + new Pods
  # ② On which port?
  ports:
    - name: http
      port: 80
      targetPort: 8080
What each block does
  • ① What to run? → replicas, selector, matchLabels, app, template, metadata
  • ② How to replace the old Pods? → strategy, type
  • ③ How fast and how safe? → rollingUpdate, maxSurge, maxUnavailable, minReadySeconds, progressDeadlineSeconds, paused
  • ④ What to keep for going back? → revisionHistoryLimit, apiVersion, kind, metadata, name, namespace
  • ① Which Pods get traffic? → selector, app
  • ② On which port? → ports, name, port, targetPort

Deploymentdeploy/02-rolling-update/rolling-profiles.yaml
In one sentence

Three services, three surge/unavailable profiles.

rolling-profiles.yamlkubectl apply -f
# Three real Jahez services, three RollingUpdate profiles
# ── Profile 1 · zero-capacity-loss: checkout must never dip ──
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: checkout-service-deployment
  namespace: jahez-prod
spec:
  # ① What to run?
  replicas: 4
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: checkout-service
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: checkout-service
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: checkout
          image: ghcr.io/jahez/checkout-service:v5.2.1
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /ready
              port: 8080
  # ② How to replace?
  strategy:
    type: RollingUpdate
    # ③ How fast and how safe?
    rollingUpdate:
      maxSurge: 1# ceiling 5 Pods
      maxUnavailable: 0# floor 4 available
  minReadySeconds: 15
---
# ── Profile 2 · balanced: the default for menu-service ──
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: menu-service-deployment
  namespace: jahez-prod
spec:
  # ① What to run?
  replicas: 4
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: menu-service
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: menu-service
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: menu
          image: ghcr.io/jahez/menu-service:v2.4.0
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /ready
              port: 8080
  # ② How to replace?
  strategy:
    type: RollingUpdate
    # ③ How fast and how safe?
    rollingUpdate:
      maxSurge: 25%# 25% of 4 = 1 (rounded up)
      maxUnavailable: 25%# 25% of 4 = 1 (rounded down)
---
# ── Profile 3 · fast: a stateless cache with spare node headroom ──
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: menu-cache-deployment
  namespace: jahez-prod
spec:
  # ① What to run?
  replicas: 4
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: menu-cache
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: menu-cache
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: cache
          image: ghcr.io/jahez/menu-cache:v1.3.0
          readinessProbe:
            tcpSocket:
              port: 6380
  # ② How to replace?
  strategy:
    type: RollingUpdate
    # ③ How fast and how safe?
    rollingUpdate:
      maxSurge: 100%# all 4 new Pods at once (8 total)
      maxUnavailable: 50%# may drop to 2 available
What each block does
  • ① What to run? → replicas, selector, matchLabels, app, template, metadata
  • ② How to replace? → strategy, type
  • ③ How fast and how safe? → rollingUpdate, maxSurge, maxUnavailable, minReadySeconds, apiVersion, kind
  • ① What to run? → replicas, selector, matchLabels, app, template, metadata
  • ② How to replace? → strategy, type
  • ③ How fast and how safe? → rollingUpdate, maxSurge, maxUnavailable, apiVersion, kind, metadata
  • ① What to run? → replicas, selector, matchLabels, app, template, metadata
  • ② How to replace? → strategy, type
  • ③ How fast and how safe? → rollingUpdate, maxSurge, maxUnavailable

# ── BLUE · current ──
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: menu-blue-deployment
  namespace: jahez-prod
spec:
  # ① Two full copies?
  replicas: 4
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: menu-service
      version: blue
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: menu-service
        version: blue
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: menu
          image: ghcr.io/jahez/menu-service:v1.9.3
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /ready
              port: 8080
---
# ── GREEN · next ──
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: menu-green-deployment
  namespace: jahez-prod
spec:
  # ① Two full copies?
  replicas: 4
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: menu-service
      version: green
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: menu-service
        version: green
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: menu
          image: ghcr.io/jahez/menu-service:v2.4.0
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /ready
              port: 8080
---
# ── ACTIVE · the Service users hit ──
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: menu-active-service
  namespace: jahez-prod
spec:
  # ② Who gets live traffic?
  selector:
    app: menu-service
    version: blue                        # flip to green = the cutover; flip back = rollback
  ports:
    - port: 80
      targetPort: 8080
---
# ── PREVIEW · QA only, no users ──
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: menu-preview-service
  namespace: jahez-prod
spec:
  # ③ How do I test green first?
  selector:
    app: menu-service
    version: green
  ports:
    - port: 80
      targetPort: 8080

SCRIPTdeploy/03-blue-green/cutover.sh
In one sentence

The scripted cutover: deploy, smoke, flip, soak, retire.

cutover.shbash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
NS=jahez-prod
# ── 1) deploy green and wait until every Pod is Ready ──
kubectl -n $NS apply -f menu-blue-green.yaml
kubectl -n $NS rollout status deploy/menu-green-deployment --timeout=180s
# ── 2) smoke-test green through the preview Service (no users yet) ──
kubectl -n $NS run smoke-pod --rm -i --restart=Never --image=curlimages/curl -- \
  curl -fsS http://menu-preview-service/ready || { echo "green failed smoke"; exit 1; }
# ── 3) the cutover: flip the active Service selector (atomic) ──
kubectl -n $NS patch svc menu-active-service --type merge \
  -p '{"spec":{"selector":{"app":"menu-service","version":"green"}}}'
# ── 4) soak; blue stays up for instant rollback ──
sleep 300
# ── 5) retire blue ──
kubectl -n $NS scale deploy/menu-blue-deployment --replicas=0
# ROLLBACK any time before step 5:
# kubectl -n $NS patch svc menu-active-service --type merge -p '{"spec":{"selector":{"version":"blue"}}}'

    In one sentence

    Argo CD Application that syncs this folder.

    menu-blue-green-application.yamlkubectl apply -f
    # Argo CD watches the repo folder; the cutover is a one-line commit to menu-blue-green.yaml
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: Application
metadata:
  name: menu-blue-green-application
  namespace: argocd
spec:
  project: default
  # ① Where is the desired state?
  source:
    repoURL: https://github.com/jahez/menu-service.git
    targetRevision: main
    path: deploy/03-blue-green
  # ② Where does it go?
  destination:
    server: https://kubernetes.default.svc
    namespace: jahez-prod
  # ③ How is it kept in sync?
  syncPolicy:
    automated:
      prune: true
      selfHeal: true# a manual kubectl patch is reverted to git
    What each block does
    • ① Where is the desired state? → source, repoURL, targetRevision, path
    • ② Where does it go? → destination, server, namespace
    • ③ How is it kept in sync? → syncPolicy, automated, prune, selfHeal

    Deployment · Servicedeploy/04-canary/menu-canary.yaml
    In one sentence

    Replica-ratio canary: 3 stable + 1 canary behind one Service.

    menu-canary.yamlkubectl apply -f
    # Replica-ratio canary: 3 stable + 1 canary = 25% of requests on v2
# ── STABLE ──
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: menu-stable-deployment
  namespace: jahez-prod
spec:
  # ① Two tracks?
  replicas: 3# 3 of 4 = 75%
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: menu-service
      track: stable
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: menu-service
        track: stable
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: menu
          image: ghcr.io/jahez/menu-service:v1.9.3
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /ready
              port: 8080
---
# ── CANARY ──
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: menu-canary-deployment
  namespace: jahez-prod
spec:
  # ① Two tracks?
  replicas: 1# 1 of 4 = 25%: raise to widen
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: menu-service
      track: canary
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: menu-service
        track: canary
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: menu
          image: ghcr.io/jahez/menu-service:v2.4.0
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /ready
              port: 8080
---
# ── SHARED SERVICE ──
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: menu-service
  namespace: jahez-prod
spec:
  # ② How is traffic split?
  selector:
    app: menu-service                    # no track key: load-balances over all 4 Pods
  ports:
    - port: 80
      targetPort: 8080
    What each block does
    • ① Two tracks? → replicas, selector, matchLabels, app, track, template
    • ① Two tracks? → replicas, selector, matchLabels, app, track, template
    • ② How is traffic split? → selector, app, ports, port, targetPort

# ── STABLE ──
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: menu-stable-deployment
  namespace: jahez-prod
spec:
  replicas: 4
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: menu-service
      track: stable
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: menu-service
        track: stable
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: menu
          image: ghcr.io/jahez/menu-service:v1.9.3
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /ready
              port: 8080
---
# ── CANARY ──
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: menu-canary-deployment
  namespace: jahez-prod
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: menu-service
      track: canary
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: menu-service
        track: canary
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: menu
          image: ghcr.io/jahez/menu-service:v2.4.0
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /ready
              port: 8080
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: menu-service
  namespace: jahez-prod
spec:
  selector:
    app: menu-service
  ports:
    - name: http
      port: 80
      targetPort: 8080
---
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1
kind: DestinationRule
metadata:
  name: menu-destination-rule
  namespace: jahez-prod
spec:
  host: menu-service
  # ① Which Pods form each subset?
  subsets:
    - name: stable
      labels:
        track: stable
    - name: canary
      labels:
        track: canary
---
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1
kind: VirtualService
metadata:
  name: menu-virtual-service
  namespace: jahez-prod
spec:
  hosts:
    - menu-service
  http:
    - name: primary
      # ② What share does each subset get?
      route:
        - destination:
            host: menu-service
            subset: stable
          weight: 75# patch these two weights to move traffic
        - destination:
            host: menu-service
            subset: canary
          weight: 25# exact %, independent of Pod count
    What each block does
    • ① Which Pods form each subset? → subsets, name, labels, track, apiVersion, kind

    SCRIPTdeploy/04-canary/canary-replica-ratio.sh
    In one sentence

    Scripted 25 → 50 → 75 → 100 by scaling.

    canary-replica-ratio.shbash
    #!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
NS=jahez-prod
step(){ # $1 = canary replicas, $2 = stable replicas (total stays 4)
  kubectl -n $NS scale deploy/menu-canary-deployment --replicas=$1
  kubectl -n $NS scale deploy/menu-stable-deployment --replicas=$2
  echo "canary ~$(( $1 * 100 / ($1 + $2) ))% -- baking"; }
step 1 3; sleep 600     # 25%: check error rate, p99, checkout success
step 2 2; sleep 600     # 50%
step 3 1; sleep 600     # 75%
step 4 0                # 100%: canary is the new stable
# ROLLBACK at any step:
# kubectl -n $NS scale deploy/menu-canary-deployment --replicas=0
# kubectl -n $NS scale deploy/menu-stable-deployment --replicas=4
    ⌘ Commands for this file
    bash deploy/04-canary/canary-replica-ratio.sh

      SCRIPTdeploy/04-canary/canary-weighted.sh
      In one sentence

      Scripted 1 → 5 → 25 → 50 → 100 by weights.

      canary-weighted.shbash
      #!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
NS=jahez-prod
set_weight(){ # $1 = canary %
  kubectl -n $NS patch vs menu-virtual-service --type json -p "[
    {\"op\":\"replace\",\"path\":\"/spec/http/0/route/0/weight\",\"value\":$((100-$1))},
    {\"op\":\"replace\",\"path\":\"/spec/http/0/route/1/weight\",\"value\":$1}]"
  echo "canary at $1%"; }
set_weight 1;  sleep 600     # tiny exposure first
set_weight 5;  sleep 600
set_weight 25; sleep 600
set_weight 50; sleep 600
set_weight 100               # promoted; rollback = set_weight 0

apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: menu-main-ingress
  namespace: jahez-prod
spec:
  ingressClassName: nginx
  rules:
    - host: menu.jahez.sa
      http:
        paths:

---
# ── Canary Ingress: x-jahez-beta: true goes to menu-b-service ──
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: menu-b-header-ingress
  namespace: jahez-prod
  annotations:
    # ① Which slice does the overlay capture?
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/canary: "true"
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/canary-by-header: "x-jahez-beta"
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/canary-by-header-value: "true"
spec:
  ingressClassName: nginx
  rules:
    - host: menu.jahez.sa                # same host + path as the main Ingress
      http:
        paths:
          - path: /
            pathType: Prefix
            backend:
              service:
                name: menu-b-service     # ② where the slice goes
                port:
                  number: 80

apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1
kind: Gateway
metadata:
  name: jahez-public-gateway
  namespace: istio-system
spec:
  # ① Which proxy pods receive the traffic?
  selector:
    istio: ingressgateway
  # ② Which hosts and ports are open?
  servers:
    - port:
        number: 443
        name: https
        protocol: HTTPS
      hosts:
        - "jahez-prod/menu.jahez.sa"
      tls:
        mode: SIMPLE
        credentialName: menu-jahez-sa-tls-secret   # issued by cert-manager in istio-system

        In one sentence

        One VirtualService: header rule first, default last.

        ab-header-istio.yamlkubectl apply -f
        apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1
kind: VirtualService
metadata:
  name: menu-ab-virtual-service
  namespace: jahez-prod
spec:
  hosts:
    - menu.jahez.sa
  gateways:
    - istio-system/jahez-public-gateway
  http:
    # ① Rule 1 · does the request match?
    - match:
        - headers:
            x-jahez-beta:
              exact: "true"
      route:
        - destination:
            host: menu-b-service         # header equals "true"
    # ② Rule 2 · no match: the default
    - route:
        - destination:
            host: menu-a-service
        What each block does
        • ① Rule 1 · does the request match? → match, headers, x-jahez-beta, exact, route, destination
        • ② Rule 2 · no match: the default → route, destination, host

kind: Deployment

spec:

# ── v2 · shadow, answers nobody (isolated in 7.2) ──
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: menu-v2-shadow-deployment
  namespace: jahez-prod
spec:
  replicas: 4# sized for 100% mirrored load
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: menu-service
      version: v2
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: menu-service
        version: v2
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: menu
          image: ghcr.io/jahez/menu-service:v2.4.0
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /ready
              port: 8080
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: menu-service
  namespace: jahez-prod
spec:
  selector:
    app: menu-service
  ports:
    - name: http
      port: 80
      targetPort: 8080
---
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1
kind: DestinationRule
metadata:
  name: menu-destination-rule
  namespace: jahez-prod
spec:
  host: menu-service
  # ① Which Pods are live and which are the shadow?
  subsets:
    - name: live
      labels:
        version: v1
    - name: shadow
      labels:
        version: v2
---
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1
kind: VirtualService
metadata:
  name: menu-mirror-virtual-service
  namespace: jahez-prod
spec:
  hosts:
    - menu-service
  http:
    - route:
        # ② Who answers the user?
        - destination:
            host: menu-service
            subset: live
          weight: 100
      # ③ Who gets a copy?
      mirror:
        host: menu-service
        subset: shadow
      # ④ How much is copied?
      mirrorPercentage:
        value: 100.0# start at 10.0 in production
        What each block does
        • ① Which Pods are live and which are the shadow? → subsets, name, labels, version, apiVersion, kind
        • ② Who answers the user? → destination, host, subset, weight
        • ③ Who gets a copy? → mirror, host, subset
        • ④ How much is copied? → mirrorPercentage, value

apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: menu-shadow-config-map
  namespace: jahez-prod
data:
  # ① Which database?
  ORDERS_DB_HOST: "orders-shadow-db-rw.jahez-shadow.svc"    # restored nightly copy
  # ③ Where do notifications go?
  NOTIFY_URL: "http://notification-sink-service.jahez-shadow.svc/discard"
  SHADOW_MODE: "true"                                       # app skips outbound webhooks
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata:
  name: mada-sandbox-secret
  namespace: jahez-prod
type: Opaque
stringData:
  # ② Which payment keys?
  MADA_API_KEY: "sandbox-key-replace-me"                    # never the live key
  MADA_BASE_URL: "https://sandbox.mada.example/api"
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: menu-v2-shadow-deployment
  namespace: jahez-prod
spec:
  replicas: 4
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: menu-service
      version: v2
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: menu-service
        version: v2
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: menu
          image: ghcr.io/jahez/menu-service:v2.4.0
          envFrom:
            - configMapRef:
                name: menu-shadow-config-map
            - secretRef:
                name: mada-sandbox-secret
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /ready
              port: 8080
---
# ④ What if the app ignores the config? Block egress to production anyway.
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: menu-shadow-network-policy
  namespace: jahez-prod
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: menu-service
      version: v2
  policyTypes:
    - Egress
  egress:
    - to:                                # only the shadow namespace
        - namespaceSelector:
            matchLabels:
              kubernetes.io/metadata.name: jahez-shadow
    - to:                                # and DNS
        - namespaceSelector:
            matchLabels:
              kubernetes.io/metadata.name: kube-system
      ports:
        - protocol: UDP
          port: 53
        What each block does

        • ② Which payment keys? → MADA_API_KEY, MADA_BASE_URL, apiVersion, kind, metadata, name

        menu-rollout-blue-green.yamlkubectl apply -f
        apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: Rollout                            # replaces the Deployment object
metadata:
  name: menu-rollout
  namespace: jahez-prod
spec:
  # ① What to run?
  replicas: 4
  revisionHistoryLimit: 5
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: menu-service
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: menu-service
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: menu
          image: ghcr.io/jahez/menu-service:v2.4.0
          ports:
            - containerPort: 8080
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /ready
              port: 8080
  strategy:
    blueGreen:
      # ② Which Services does Argo repoint?
      activeService: menu-active-service       # users
      previewService: menu-preview-service     # QA, before promotion
      # ③ Who decides the flip?
      autoPromotionEnabled: false# wait for kubectl argo rollouts promote
      prePromotionAnalysis:                    # must pass BEFORE the flip
        templates:
          - templateName: smoke-analysis-template
        args:
          - name: service-name
            value: menu-preview-service
      postPromotionAnalysis:                   # watched AFTER the flip; fail = auto-abort
        templates:
          - templateName: success-rate-analysis-template
      # ④ How long is going back instant?
      scaleDownDelaySeconds: 300# old ReplicaSet kept 5 min
---

kind: Service
metadata:
  name: menu-active-service
  namespace: jahez-prod
spec:
  selector:
    app: menu-service                    # Argo adds rollouts-pod-template-hash
  ports:
    - port: 80
      targetPort: 8080
---

metadata:
  name: menu-preview-service
  namespace: jahez-prod
spec:
  selector:
    app: menu-service
  ports:
    - port: 80
      targetPort: 8080

        menu-rollout-canary.yamlkubectl apply -f
        apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: Rollout
metadata:
  name: menu-rollout
  namespace: jahez-prod
spec:
  # ① What to run?
  replicas: 4
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: menu-service
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: menu-service
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: menu
          image: ghcr.io/jahez/menu-service:v2.4.0
          ports:
            - containerPort: 8080
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /ready
              port: 8080
  strategy:
    canary:
      # ② Which Services and routes does Argo control?
      stableService: menu-stable-service
      canaryService: menu-canary-service
      trafficRouting:
        istio:
          virtualService:
            name: menu-virtual-service
            routes:
              - primary
      # ③ What is the step plan?
      steps:
        - setWeight: 25
        - pause:
            duration: 10m
        - analysis:
            templates:
              - templateName: success-rate-analysis-template
        - setWeight: 50
        - pause:
            duration: 10m
        - setWeight: 75
        - pause:
            duration: 10m
        - setWeight: 100

  name: menu-canary-service
  namespace: jahez-prod
spec:
  selector:
    app: menu-service                    # Argo adds the canary pod-template-hash

      targetPort: 8080
---
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1
kind: VirtualService
metadata:
  name: menu-virtual-service
  namespace: jahez-prod
spec:
  hosts:
    - menu.jahez.sa
  gateways:
    - istio-system/jahez-public-gateway
  http:
    - name: primary                      # Argo rewrites these weights each step
      route:
        - destination:
            host: menu-stable-service
          weight: 100
        - destination:
            host: menu-canary-service
          weight: 0

        # ── Gate 1 · smoke test the preview Service with a Job ──
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: AnalysisTemplate
metadata:
  name: smoke-analysis-template
  namespace: jahez-prod
spec:
  # ① What can the caller pass in?
  args:
    - name: service-name
  metrics:
    - name: smoke
      # ③ When is it a pass?
      count: 1
      failureLimit: 0
      # ② Where does the measurement come from?
      provider:
        job:
          spec:
            backoffLimit: 0
            template:
              spec:
                restartPolicy: Never
                containers:
                  - name: smoke
                    image: curlimages/curl:8.10.1
                    args:
                      - "-fsS"
                      - "http://{{args.service-name}}/ready"
---
# ── Gate 2 · live success rate from Prometheus ──
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: AnalysisTemplate
metadata:
  name: success-rate-analysis-template
  namespace: jahez-prod
spec:
  metrics:
    - name: success-rate
      # ③ When is it a pass?
      interval: 1m
      count: 5# 5 measurements
      successCondition: result[0] >= 0.99  # at least 99% non-5xx
      failureLimit: 2# 3rd failure aborts
      # ② Where does the measurement come from?
      provider:
        prometheus:
          address: http://prometheus-service.monitoring:9090
          query: |
            sum(rate(http_requests_total{app="menu-service",code!~"5.."}[2m]))
            /
            sum(rate(http_requests_total{app="menu-service"}[2m]))
        What each block does

        • ③ When is it a pass? → interval, count, successCondition, failureLimit
        • ② Where does the measurement come from? → provider, prometheus, address, query

        Canary · Deploymentdeploy/flagger/menu-canary-flagger.yaml
        In one sentence

        Deployment + Canary: Flagger ramps +10% a minute up to 50%.

        menu-canary-flagger.yamlkubectl apply -f
        apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: menu-service-deployment
  namespace: jahez-prod
spec:
  replicas: 4
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: menu-service
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: menu-service
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: menu
          image: ghcr.io/jahez/menu-service:v2.4.0
          ports:
            - containerPort: 8080
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /ready
              port: 8080
---
apiVersion: flagger.app/v1beta1
kind: Canary
metadata:
  name: menu-service-canary
  namespace: jahez-prod
spec:
  provider: istio
  # ① Which workload does Flagger take over?
  targetRef:
    apiVersion: apps/v1
    kind: Deployment
    name: menu-service-deployment         # Flagger clones it to -primary
  # ② Which Services does it generate?
  service:
    name: menu-service                    # creates menu-service, -primary, -canary
    port: 80
    targetPort: 8080
  # ③ How does the ramp run?
  analysis:
    interval: 1m                          # one loop per minute
    threshold: 5# 5 failed checks = rollback
    maxWeight: 50# ramp up to 50% ...
    stepWeight: 10# ... in +10% steps, then promote
    # ④ What counts as healthy?
    metrics:
      - name: request-success-rate
        thresholdRange:
          min: 99# at least 99%
        interval: 1m
      - name: request-duration
        thresholdRange:
          max: 500# p99 at most 500 ms
        interval: 1m
    webhooks:
      - name: load-test
        url: http://flagger-loadtester.test/
        metadata:
          cmd: "hey -z 1m -q 10 -c 2 http://menu-service-canary.jahez-prod/"
        What each block does
        • ① Which workload does Flagger take over? → targetRef, apiVersion, kind, name
        • ② Which Services does it generate? → service, name, port, targetPort
        • ③ How does the ramp run? → analysis, interval, threshold, maxWeight, stepWeight
        • ④ What counts as healthy? → metrics, name, thresholdRange, min, interval, max

        ▲ One folder at a time

        Several folders reuse names such as menu-service and menu-virtual-service. They are alternatives for the same app; applying two folders together would make them overwrite each other.

        2.3 · 2. Architecture and workflows

        Internal order: the rollout loop

        In one sentence

        A RollingUpdate is a loop: store the change, make a new ReplicaSet, surge one Pod, schedule, start, wait for Ready and Available, drain one old Pod, repeat.

        Trace menu-service-deployment (4 replicas, maxSurge 1, maxUnavailable 0, minReadySeconds 10) from v1.9.3 to v2.4.0. Each stage shows what comes in, which field of menu-service-deployment.yaml drives it, and what changes in etcd.

        ◆ About the outputs

        Outputs are example outputs from a cluster shaped like jahez-prod; hashes and IPs will differ on yours.

        The rollout loop · stage 0 → ⑩11 steps

        Slow-start: why 20 Pods are not created in one burst

        Stage ④ adds one Pod at a time here. When a ReplicaSet must add many Pods at once — Recreate scaling a 20-replica worker from 0, or the fast profile surging 100% — the ReplicaSet controller still batches the creates. With Recreate it happens in two phases:

        Phase 1 — terminate (parallel)

        • Old ReplicaSet scales to 0; all 20 old pods get SIGTERM at once.
        • Controller waits until every one has fully terminated.
        • This whole window is the downtime gap.

        Phase 2 — create (slow-start batched)

        • New ReplicaSet scales to 20 in one scale op.
        • But the RS controller creates pods in exponential batches, not one flat burst.
        • Readiness does not gate creation (that's RollingUpdate, not this).

        The ReplicaSet controller uses a slow-start safeguard (SlowStartInitialBatchSize = 1): it creates pods in concurrent batches that double on each success — and only proceeds to the next batch if the previous one's API creates succeeded.

        slow-start batching · 20 replicascontroller internals
        # the RS controller scales 0 → 20 in these concurrent batches:
batch 1 → 1  pod    # if it fails (bad image / webhook reject) → stop here, fail fast
batch 2 → 2  pods   # 3 created so far
batch 3 → 4  pods   # 7
batch 4 → 8  pods   # 15
batch 5 → 5  pods   # 20 (capped at the remainder)
# within a batch the creates are concurrent; batches run in quick succession
# — roughly one reconcile cycle, so it *looks* effectively parallel
        ◆ Why batch instead of one burst?

        Defensive throttling. If the pod template is broken — unpullable image, an admission webhook that rejects it — the controller fails after batch 1 instead of spamming the API server with 20 doomed creates. It also keeps controller QPS within the client rate limits.

        ▲ "Created" ≠ "Running"

        Even once all 20 Pod objects exist, they still have to be scheduled and have images pulled by each node's kubelet. On a small cluster you'll see them come up in waves because the nodes can't pull and start 20 containers at once — so actual startup parallelism is bounded by node capacity and image-pull throughput, not by the Deployment controller.

        Object by object: logic, full YAML, every property, deep dives, then every command.
        3.0 · 3. Native strategies · Deployment

        How a Deployment rollout works

        In one sentence

        A Deployment owns one ReplicaSet per template version and moves replicas from the old one to the new one, at the pace spec.strategy allows.

        ① The logic, read first

        You change the template; the Deployment changes the ReplicaSets; the ReplicaSets change the Pods. Every field of a Deployment answers one of four questions.

        Question it answersFieldsThink of it as
        ① What to run?replicas · selector · templatethe order: how many, of what
        ② How to replace the old Pods?strategy.typedemolish first, or build beside
        ③ How fast and how safe?maxSurge · maxUnavailable · minReadySeconds · progressDeadlineSeconds · pausedthe speed limit and the watchdog
        ④ What to keep for going back?revisionHistoryLimitthe undo stack
        Familyapps/v1 workload
        Scopenamespace
        OwnsReplicaSets → Pods
        Typical useevery stateless Jahez service
        ② Full YAML
        menu-service-deployment.yamlkubectl apply -f
        apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: menu-service-deployment
  namespace: jahez-prod
  labels:
    app: menu-service
  annotations:
    kubernetes.io/change-cause: "v2.4.0 · new menu layout"   # shown by rollout history
spec:
  # ① What to run?
  replicas: 4
  selector:                              # immutable after create
    matchLabels:
      app: menu-service
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: menu-service                # must match the selector
    spec:
      terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 30
      containers:
        - name: menu
          image: ghcr.io/jahez/menu-service:v2.4.0   # changing this starts a rollout
          ports:
            - containerPort: 8080
          resources:
            requests:
              cpu: "250m"
              memory: "1Gi"
            limits:
              cpu: "500m"
              memory: "3Gi"
          readinessProbe:                # the gate every rollout waits on
            httpGet:
              path: /ready
              port: 8080
            periodSeconds: 5
  # ② How to replace the old Pods?
  strategy:
    type: RollingUpdate
    # ③ How fast and how safe?
    rollingUpdate:
      maxSurge: 1# at most replicas + 1 = 5 Pods
      maxUnavailable: 0# never fewer than 4 available
  minReadySeconds: 10# Ready for 10s before it counts
  progressDeadlineSeconds: 300# no progress for 5 min = failed
  paused: false
  # ④ What to keep for going back?
  revisionHistoryLimit: 10# old ReplicaSets kept for rollout undo
---

kind: Service

  namespace: jahez-prod
spec:
  # ① Which Pods get traffic?
  selector:
    app: menu-service                    # no version key: spans old + new Pods
  # ② On which port?
  ports:
    - name: http
      port: 80
      targetPort: 8080

        3.1 · 3. Native strategies · Deployment

        Recreate

        In one sentence

        Recreate stops every old Pod first and only then starts the new ones, so two versions never overlap and there is a gap with zero Pods.

        Standard definition

        A deployment strategy in which all running instances of the current version are terminated before any instances of the new version are created. Exactly one version exists at any time, at the cost of a window of full unavailability.

        ① The logic, read first
        Question it answersFieldsThink of it as
        ② How to replace?strategy.type: Recreatedemolish, then rebuild
        ① What comes back?replicas · templatethe new building
        ④ Can I go back?revisionHistoryLimityes, through another gap

        When it is the right call

        • Schema changes that are not backward-compatible: v1 cannot run against v2's database shape.
        • Singletons: a worker holding an exclusive lock or writing one file.
        • Dev and batch jobs where seconds of downtime do not matter.
        ✕ Never on a customer path

        Every in-flight request fails during the gap. Keep Recreate off the menu and checkout APIs; use it for internal workers and migrations behind a maintenance flag.

        Recreate rollout — menu-migrator v1 → v24 steps
        1

        Steady state on v1

        Two v1 Pods serve traffic. The Service endpoint list points at both.

        ‹ Back1 / 4
        2

        Scale old ReplicaSet to 0

        The controller deletes both v1 Pods at once. Endpoints empty out — this is the downtime gap. Requests now get connection-refused or a 503 from the Service.

        2 / 4
        3

        Create new ReplicaSet Pods

        Only after the old Pods are gone does the v2 ReplicaSet scale up. The Pods start, pull the image, and begin their readiness probe.

        3 / 4
        4

        v2 Ready — gap closes

        When both v2 Pods pass readiness they're added to Endpoints and traffic resumes. The whole window from step 2 to here is your outage.

        4 / 4Done ✓

        With 20 replicas the new Pods are not created in one burst: see slow-start batching in 2.3 →

        ② Full YAML
        menu-migrator-deployment.yamlkubectl apply -f
        # Internal migration worker: one version at a time, a short gap is acceptable
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: menu-migrator-deployment
  namespace: jahez-prod
  labels:
    app: menu-migrator
    tier: backend
spec:
  # ① What to run?
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: menu-migrator
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: menu-migrator
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: migrator
          image: ghcr.io/jahez/menu-migrator:v2
          ports:
            - containerPort: 8080
          env:
            - name: DB_HOST
              value: "postgres-rw.jahez-prod.svc"
            - name: REGION
              value: "me-central-1"
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /healthz
              port: 8080
            initialDelaySeconds: 5
            periodSeconds: 5
  # ② How to replace the old Pods?
  strategy:
    type: Recreate                       # kill all, then create all; no rollingUpdate block
  # ④ What to keep for going back?
  revisionHistoryLimit: 5

kind: Service
metadata:
  name: menu-migrator-service
  namespace: jahez-prod
spec:
  selector:                              # version-agnostic: matches v1 and v2
    app: menu-migrator
  ports:
    - port: 80
      targetPort: 8080

        Memory footprint

        3.2 · 3. Native strategies · Deployment

        RollingUpdate

        In one sentence

        RollingUpdate brings new Pods up before old ones go down, one window at a time, so capacity never falls below your floor.

        Standard definition

        A deployment strategy that incrementally replaces instances of the old version with the new one, a controlled few at a time, keeping enough instances available throughout. The pace is bounded by maxSurge and maxUnavailable.

        ① The logic, read first
        Question it answersFieldsThink of it as
        ③ How far above?maxSurgeextra lanes you may open
        ③ How far below?maxUnavailablelanes you may close
        ② Which strategy?type: RollingUpdatebuild beside, then demolish
        ▲ The arithmetic

        Pods stay inside a window: at most replicas + maxSurge total, at least replicas − maxUnavailable available. 4 / 1 / 0 → never fewer than 4, never more than 5.

        GoalmaxSurgemaxUnavailableBehaviourJahez service
        Zero-capacity-loss10Always ≥ replicas available. Safest, slowest.checkout-service
        Balanced25%25%Good speed, tolerates a small dip.menu-service
        Fast100%50%Doubles capacity briefly, ~one window.menu-cache
        RollingUpdate — menu-service, replicas 4 · surge 1 · unavailable 06 steps
        1

        Steady: 4× v1 Ready

        Four v1 Pods spread across three nodes. All in Endpoints, all serving.

        ‹ Back1 / 6
        2

        Surge +1: one v2 starts

        Because maxSurge: 1, the controller creates a 5th Pod on the new ReplicaSet. It's not Ready yet, so it gets no traffic. All four v1 still serve — maxUnavailable: 0 holds the floor.

        2 / 6
        3

        v2 Ready → drain one v1

        The new Pod passes readiness and joins Endpoints. Now there are 5 Ready, so the controller retires one v1 to return to the window. Both versions briefly serve traffic together.

        3 / 6
        4

        Next surge window

        The loop repeats: another v2 comes up, more v1 drain. The mix shifts toward v2 one window at a time.

        4 / 6
        5

        Last v1 draining

        Four v2 are Ready and serving; the final v1 Pod terminates gracefully (drains its in-flight requests over terminationGracePeriodSeconds).

        5 / 6
        6

        Rollout complete

        The new ReplicaSet owns all 4 replicas; the old one is scaled to 0 but kept for rollback. kubectl rollout status returns success.

        6 / 6Done ✓

        Same rollout, different tuning

        Balanced — replicas 4 · maxSurge 25% (=1) · maxUnavailable 25% (=1)5 steps
        1

        Steady: 4× v1 Ready

        Same starting point. Window for this profile: ceiling replicas+1 = 5, floor replicas−1 = 3 available.

        ‹ Back1 / 5
        2

        Surge AND drain in the same window

        Because maxUnavailable: 1 permits dropping to 3 available, the controller doesn’t wait — it creates a v2 and terminates a v1 at the same time. Now: 3 v1 Ready, 1 v1 draining, 1 v2 starting. Total 5 (ceiling), available 3 (floor).

        2 / 5
        3

        First v2 Ready → next pair churns

        As the new Pod passes readiness, the drained v1 is gone and the controller immediately starts another v2 and drains another v1. Two Pods are always in flight — that’s why it’s faster than the zero-loss profile.

        3 / 5
        4

        Mostly v2

        Three v2 Ready and serving; the last v1 drains while the final v2 warms up. Capacity has dipped to 3 (75%) at points — the trade you accepted for speed.

        4 / 5
        5

        Done in fewer windows

        All 4 replicas on v2. Reached the end faster than surge 1 / unavailable 0 because surge and drain overlapped — at the cost of a tolerated 25% capacity dip.

        5 / 5Done ✓
        Fast — replicas 4 · maxSurge 100% (=4) · maxUnavailable 50% (=2)4 steps
        1

        Steady: 4× v1 Ready

        Window for this profile is wide open: ceiling replicas×2 = 8, floor replicas−2 = 2 available.

        ‹ Back1 / 4
        2

        Surge all 4 at once + drain 2

        maxSurge: 4 lets the controller stand up all four v2 Pods simultaneously (8 Pods total — double capacity), while maxUnavailable: 2 lets it drain 2 v1 right away. 2 v1 Ready, 2 draining, 4 v2 starting. Available 2 (floor), total 8 (ceiling).

        2 / 4
        3

        v2 batch goes Ready

        All four v2 pass readiness together; the last two v1 drain. For a moment you have 4 v2 serving plus 2 v1 terminating.

        3 / 4
        4

        Done in ~one window

        4 v2, finished almost in a single sweep. Fastest of the three — but it needed headroom for 8 Pods and accepted running at half capacity (2 serving) mid-roll. Great for stateless caches, risky on a tight resource budget.

        4 / 4Done ✓
        ◆ Reading the three together

        Zero-loss never drops below 4 serving (1 Pod in flight). Balanced tolerates 3 to keep 2 Pods churning. Fast doubles to 8 and accepts 2 to finish in one sweep.

        ② Full YAML
        rolling-profiles.yamlkubectl apply -f
        # Three real Jahez services, three RollingUpdate profiles
# ── Profile 1 · zero-capacity-loss: checkout must never dip ──
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: checkout-service-deployment
  namespace: jahez-prod
spec:
  # ① What to run?
  replicas: 4
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: checkout-service
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: checkout-service
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: checkout
          image: ghcr.io/jahez/checkout-service:v5.2.1
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /ready
              port: 8080
  # ② How to replace?
  strategy:
    type: RollingUpdate
    # ③ How fast and how safe?
    rollingUpdate:
      maxSurge: 1# ceiling 5 Pods
      maxUnavailable: 0# floor 4 available
  minReadySeconds: 15
---
# ── Profile 2 · balanced: the default for menu-service ──
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: menu-service-deployment
  namespace: jahez-prod
spec:
  # ① What to run?
  replicas: 4
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: menu-service
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: menu-service
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: menu
          image: ghcr.io/jahez/menu-service:v2.4.0
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /ready
              port: 8080
  # ② How to replace?
  strategy:
    type: RollingUpdate
    # ③ How fast and how safe?
    rollingUpdate:
      maxSurge: 25%# 25% of 4 = 1 (rounded up)
      maxUnavailable: 25%# 25% of 4 = 1 (rounded down)
---
# ── Profile 3 · fast: a stateless cache with spare node headroom ──
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: menu-cache-deployment
  namespace: jahez-prod
spec:
  # ① What to run?
  replicas: 4
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: menu-cache
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: menu-cache
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: cache
          image: ghcr.io/jahez/menu-cache:v1.3.0
          readinessProbe:
            tcpSocket:
              port: 6380
  # ② How to replace?
  strategy:
    type: RollingUpdate
    # ③ How fast and how safe?
    rollingUpdate:
      maxSurge: 100%# all 4 new Pods at once (8 total)
      maxUnavailable: 50%# may drop to 2 available

        ③ Every property
        ③ Every property
        ③ strategy.rollingUpdateobjectthe window
        maxSurgeint | %Pods allowed above replicas

        Percent is of replicas, rounded up. Higher = faster, more peak resources.

        ValueMeaning

        ④ Deep dive

        Profile 1 · zero-capacity-loss

        Limits — 3 GB/pod (cap)
        Requests — 1 GB/pod (reserved)
        Usage — 0.5–1.5 GB/pod (actual)

        Peak reserved 5 GB (+25%), one extra Pod at a time.

        Profile 2 · balanced

        Limits — 3 GB/pod (cap)
        Requests — 1 GB/pod (reserved)
        Usage — 0.5–1.5 GB/pod (actual)

        Same 5 GB peak; usage dips because only 3 Pods serve during churn.

        Profile 3 · fast

        Limits — 3 GB/pod (cap)
        Requests — 1 GB/pod (reserved)
        Usage — 0.5–1.5 GB/pod (actual)

        Peak reserved 8 GB for one short window. Budget schedulable headroom for it.

        3.3 · 3. Native strategies · Deployment

        Pacing and history fields

        In one sentence

        Four fields decide when a new Pod counts, when a rollout is declared stuck, whether it may move at all, and how far back you can undo.

        ① The logic, read first
        Question it answersFieldsThink of it as
        ① When does a new Pod count?minReadySecondsprobation period
        ② When is a rollout stuck?progressDeadlineSecondsthe watchdog
        ③ Is it allowed to move?pausedthe hand brake
        ④ How far back?revisionHistoryLimitundo stack depth
        ② Full YAML
        menu-service-pacing.yamlkubectl apply -f
        apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: menu-service-deployment
  namespace: jahez-prod
  annotations:
    kubernetes.io/change-cause: "v2.4.0 · new menu layout"
spec:
  replicas: 4
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: menu-service
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: menu-service
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: menu
          image: ghcr.io/jahez/menu-service:v2.4.0
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /ready
              port: 8080
  strategy:
    type: RollingUpdate
    rollingUpdate:
      maxSurge: 1
      maxUnavailable: 0
  # ① When does a new Pod count?
  minReadySeconds: 10# Ready for 10s without flapping
  # ② When is a rollout stuck?
  progressDeadlineSeconds: 300# sets Progressing=False after 5 min
  # ③ Is the rollout allowed to move?
  paused: false# true = template changes wait
  # ④ How far back can I go?
  revisionHistoryLimit: 10# 0 would delete every old ReplicaSet

        read why the rollout is where it is

        Read from cluster then cluster unchanged.

        • -n — namespace

        ③ Every property
        ③ Every property
        ① minReadySecondsintegerReady this long before the Pod counts as Available

        The rollout counts availableReplicas, not Ready Pods. A flapping v2 never passes the soak, so the old Pods stay.

        ValueMeaning
        0Ready = Available immediately
        10–15Jahez default for API services

        Default 0

        ② progressDeadlineSecondsintegerseconds without progress before the rollout is marked failed

        Sets condition Progressing=False, reason ProgressDeadlineExceeded. It does not roll back; rollout status exits 1 so CI can.

        Default 600

        ③ pausedbooleantrue = template changes are stored but not rolled out

        Set by kubectl rollout pause. Lets you batch image + env + resources into one rollout.

        Default false

        ④ revisionHistoryLimitintegerhow many old ReplicaSets stay at 0 replicas

        0 deletes every old ReplicaSet: rollout undo then has nothing to return to.

        Default 10

        •metadata.annotations["kubernetes.io/change-cause"]stringthe text in the CHANGE-CAUSE column of rollout history

  Available      True    MinimumReplicasAvailable
  Progressing    False   ProgressDeadlineExceeded
        ✕ When it fails progressDeadlineSeconds ≤ minReadySeconds is rejected by validation.
        3.4 · 3. Native strategies · Deployment

        Probes and graceful shutdown

        In one sentence

        Probes make a rollout safe rather than merely automatic: readiness decides when a new Pod takes traffic, preStop and the grace period decide how an old Pod leaves.

        ① The logic, read first
        Question it answersFieldsThink of it as
        ① Has it booted?startupProbethe boarding gate
        ② Can it serve now?readinessProbethe open/closed sign
        ③ Is it stuck?livenessProbethe heartbeat monitor
        ④ How does it leave?preStop · terminationGracePeriodSecondslast orders before closing
        StateMeansDriven byEffect on rollout
        RunningPID 1 is up; may still be connectingkubeletnone
        ReadyIP added to the EndpointSlicereadinessProbenecessary, not enough
        AvailableReady for minReadySecondsReady + timeropens the next window
        ✕ The classic outage

        No readinessProbe → "Ready" the instant the process starts → old Pods drained while new ones still connect to Postgres → 503s for 10–20 s.

        ② Full YAML
        menu-service-probes.yamlkubectl apply -f
        apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: menu-service-deployment
  namespace: jahez-prod
spec:
  replicas: 4
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: menu-service
  strategy:
    type: RollingUpdate
    rollingUpdate:
      maxSurge: 1
      maxUnavailable: 0
  minReadySeconds: 10
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: menu-service
    spec:
      # ④ How long may it take to stop?
      terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 30
      containers:
        - name: menu
          image: ghcr.io/jahez/menu-service:v2.4.0
          ports:
            - containerPort: 8080
          # ① Has it finished booting?
          startupProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /healthz
              port: 8080
            periodSeconds: 5
            failureThreshold: 24# up to 2 min to boot
          # ② Can it serve right now?
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /ready                # checks Postgres, Redis, Elasticsearch
              port: 8080
            periodSeconds: 5
            failureThreshold: 2
            successThreshold: 1
          # ③ Is it stuck?
          livenessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /healthz              # process only, never dependencies
              port: 8080
            periodSeconds: 10
            failureThreshold: 3
          lifecycle:
            preStop:                      # let EndpointSlice + LB catch up before SIGTERM
              exec:
                command:
                  - "sh"
                  - "-c"
                  - "sleep 5"

        ③ Every property

        Until it passes, liveness and readiness are not run. Protects slow starters from being killed.

        •failureThreshold × periodSecondsintegermaximum boot time (24 × 5 s = 2 min)

        4.0 · 4. Blue / Green

        How Blue/Green works

        In one sentence

        Run two complete copies, send all users to one, test the other privately, then flip a single Service selector to cut over, and flip it back to roll back.

        Standard definition

        A deployment strategy that maintains two production environments, one live (blue) and one idle (green), deploys the new version to the idle one and switches all traffic in a single atomic cut-over once verified.

        ① The logic, read first
        Question it answersFieldsThink of it as
        ① Two full copies?two Deployments · version labeltwo kitchens, both fully staffed
        ② Who gets live traffic?menu-active-service.spec.selectorthe front-door sign
        ③ How do I test green first?menu-preview-servicea staff-only side door
        ④ How do I go back?patch the selector backturn the sign around

        Strengths

        • Instant, atomic switch
        • Instant rollback while blue runs
        • Green tested via preview first

        Costs

        • 2× capacity during the overlap
        • Long-lived connections to blue are cut at retirement
        • DB changes must work for both colours
        Blue/Green cutover — menu-service v1 → v24 steps
        1

        Blue (v1) live

        Service selector = version: blue. Only v1 Pods are in Endpoints.

        ‹ Back1 / 4
        2

        Deploy green (v2), no traffic

        The green Deployment scales up fully. It's Ready but the production Service still selects blue, so green receives zero live traffic. Verify it through a private preview Service.

        2 / 4
        3

        Flip the selector

        One kubectl patch changes the Service selector to version: green. Endpoints swap atomically — the next request lands on v2. This is the cutover.

        3 / 4
        4

        Retire blue

        After a soak period (kept around for instant rollback), scale blue to 0 or delete it. Green is now the new blue.

        4 / 4Done ✓
        ② Full YAML
        menu-blue-green.yamlkubectl apply -f

kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: menu-blue-deployment
  namespace: jahez-prod
spec:
  # ① Two full copies?
  replicas: 4
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: menu-service
      version: blue
  template:
